vignette:
Mai had been working as a mechanic for most of her adult life, and at 76 she still spent her days in the same kind of practical, grease-scented environment that had always made sense to her. The workshop was familiar, noisy, and full of the ordinary smells of metal, oil, rubber, and dirt tracked in from outside. It was also the place where, many years ago, the stalking that changed her sense of safety had begun to feel impossible to ignore. At first it had been small things: repeated sightings of the same person near her home and workplace, a sense that she was being noticed when she did not want to be. Then it became more explicit, with the person turning up in places where Mai expected privacy, leaving her with the feeling that she could never quite tell who might be watching. What had once been a predictable daily life became something she experienced as exposed, and even after the immediate episodes had passed, the impression of being followed did not leave her. She had come to feel that the world outside her door could turn threatening without warning, and that sense of exposure settled into the ordinary movements of her day.

Over time, Mai began to notice how certain moments could bring the whole experience back with unusual force. The smell of soil after rain, or the outdoor smell that drifted in when the workshop doors were left open, could catch her off guard and make her feel suddenly tense, as if she had been pulled back into that earlier time. She could be in the middle of a workday, standing near a vehicle in the garage, and a whiff of earth from the yard or a patch of wet ground outside would make her pause and scan the surroundings. Stress itself had become another unmistakable cue for her; when demands piled up or the day felt crowded, she found herself more unsettled and more likely to feel the old fear rising without much warning. Even times that should have been pleasant could trouble her. If she felt happy or relaxed, especially in a quiet moment after finishing a job or sitting at home with her husband, she became uneasy, as though ease itself left her vulnerable. In those moments she would sense that she should not let her guard down, and the relief would be replaced by watchfulness.

Mai described that watchfulness in immediate, physical terms. She was superalert and on guard much of the time, and this did not switch off when she came inside. At home, even in rooms she had lived in for years, she remained alert to movement and sound, as if safety were never fully guaranteed by walls and a locked door. She frequently looked behind her to check whether someone might be following her, a habit that had become so automatic that she sometimes did it without intending to. On the street, in the parking lot near the garage, or even moving from one room to another at home, she would turn her head and look back, trying to make sure no one was there. She did not describe herself as panicked, but rather as constantly prepared, unable to let herself be surprised again. This was especially true when she was going about everyday tasks that used to feel routine; what had changed was not the tasks themselves but the way she moved through them, always with a part of her attention scanning behind and around her.

When Mai tried to explain what had happened, she often found herself losing the thread and unable to finish. She would start to describe the period when she felt watched, then stop, as if the details slipped out of reach before she could organize them into a clear account. There were moments when she found herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it, not because she wanted to forget exactly, but because the images came so quickly that she felt she had to move off them before they became overwhelming. What remained most readily available were vivid, almost still-like snapshots. She remembered the frightening event in her mind like photographs, with sharp, separate images rather than a smooth story: a face, a place, a moment of seeing someone where she did not expect them. These fragments felt precise but disconnected, and that made the memory difficult to speak about in a continuous way. Her account at intake was often interrupted by pauses, not from lack of willingness but from the way the memory seemed to break apart as she approached it.

By the time she sought help, Mai had grown tired of living as though danger might appear at any moment, even in the workshop she still went to and the home she shared with her husband. She came because the constant checking and alertness were wearing on her, and because she no longer wanted even brief moments of happiness to be followed by fear. What frightened her most was the possibility that she would never fully trust being outside or inside her own house again. More than anything, she hoped to feel settled enough to move through her days without looking over her shoulder, and to be able to speak about what happened without the memory breaking apart before she could finish.
